en: The Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra, also known as the Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha, having first attained the Way, was staying at Gayā in the kingdom of Magadha.

At the mountain shrine, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus; they had all previously been matted-hair sages, and were now all arhats who had accomplished what was to be done, attained mastery over their minds, realized their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and were liberated through right knowledge.

There were also ten thousand bodhisattvas who had gathered from the worlds of the ten directions, possessing great majestic virtue, having all attained the various patiences, the various dhāraṇīs, and the various profound samādhis, and being endowed with all supernatural powers.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Gandhahastin Bodhisattva, Sūradatta Bodhisattva, and Anugatajñānacaryā Bodhisattva were their leaders.
Such was the great assembly of bodhisattvas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, their count being immeasurable;
they were surrounded by a vast multitude including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the profound samādhi of all Buddhas and, observing the nature and characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are, had this thought:

"I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and acquired all-encompassing wisdom; I have laid down the heavy burdens and crossed the perilous paths of the three realms of existence; I have extinguished ignorance and attained true illumination; I have extracted the arrows of perversion and severed craving; I have completed the Dharma-boat, struck the Dharma-drum, blown the Dharma-conch, and raised the Dharma-banner; I have transformed the seeds of birth and death and revealed the nature of Nirvāṇa; I have blocked off the evil paths and opened the straight road; I have led beings away from all unwholesome karma and shown them the field of merit."
I shall now investigate: who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—is it attained by means of the body, or is it attained by means of the mind?

"If it were attained by means of the body, the body would be without cognition and without volition, like grass, trees, tiles, or stones; it is composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, sustained by clothing, food and drink, bedding, and bathing, and must inevitably return to decay, impermanence, and extinction."

This bodhi, however, exists only as a name spoken for the sake of worldly convention; it is formless, colorless, non-fixed, signless, directionless, entranceless, and pathless. It transcends all verbal expression and issues forth from the triple world; it is unseen, unheard, unperceived, and unknown; it is neither obtainable nor subject to conceptual proliferation; it is without question, without demonstration, without characters, and without the path of speech.

"If one attains it by means of the mind, the mind arises from a multitude of conditions; because it arises from conditions, it is empty like an illusion, without location, without marks, and without intrinsic nature, and is likewise non-existent. To attain bodhi within this [state], the dharmas used to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—all these dharmas are empty and exist only as names. They are spoken of only for the sake of worldly convention; they are all mere conceptualizations and discriminations, truly having nothing at all, lacking any root, and devoid of any essential substance or characteristics."
There is no grasping, no attachment, no defilement, and no renunciation; it is of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless.
Therefore, within this Dharma, there is no one who attains.
“There is no dharma to be employed, nor is there any bodhi.
To penetrate thus is what is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī was in the great assembly, standing to the right of the Buddha, holding a great precious parasol to cover the Buddha above.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, silently knowing the thought in the World-Honored One’s mind, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bodhi has such characteristics as these, how should sons and daughters of good family resolve their minds?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Good sons and good daughters, you should give rise to the mind [of awakening] in accordance with the characteristics of bodhi.
Mañjuśrī asked: “World-Honored One, how should the characteristics of bodhi be explained?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The characteristic of bodhi transcends the triple world and surpasses worldly dharmas; it is where the path of speech is cut off, and all arousal and non-arousal are extinguished—this is the arousal of bodhi."
Mañjuśrī! For this reason, a bodhisattva should extinguish all acts of generating [the mind]. To generate the bodhicitta without generating is the generation of bodhicitta.

That which generates the bodhicitta is like the suchness of the dharma-nature; its mark is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), free from discrimination, and not conditioned by body or mind—this is the generation of bodhicitta.
Not clinging to any phenomena, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither different nor identical—this is the arousal of bodhicitta.
One should arouse the mind of enlightenment in this way: like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like a shadow, like an echo, and like the moon in water.
At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Candraprabhaśrīguṇa, who had attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
He asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:
"For what purpose does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva path?"
Mañjuśrī said, “You may pose this question to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Answer the question asked by the Devaputra Candravimalaguṇatejas regarding the practice of the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī said to the devaputra: "Listen attentively; I shall now speak."
"Son of Heaven, you should know that the path of all bodhisattvas has great compassion as its root and takes sentient beings as its object.
The son of heaven asked:
"What is the root of a bodhisattva’s great compassion?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “It has a straightforward mind as its foundation.
He asked again:
“What is the foundation of the straightforward mind? He replied:
“Equanimity toward all sentient beings is its foundation.”
He asked again:
"What is the foundation of an impartial mind? He replied:
"Non-differentiated conduct is its basis.
He asked again:
"What is the basis of non-differentiated conduct?"
He replied, "It is rooted in a profound and pure mind.
He asked again:
"What is the foundation of the profound and pure mind? He replied,
"It has the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as its foundation."
He asked again:
"What is the root of the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? He replied:
"It takes the six pāramitās as its basis.
He asked again:
"What do the six pāramitās take as their basis?"
He replied, "Skillful means have wisdom as their foundation.
He asked again:
"What is the basis of skillful means and wisdom? He replied,
"Heedfulness is the basis."
He asked again:
"What is the root of heedfulness? He replied:
"The three types of wholesome conduct have their basis.
He asked again:
"What is the basis of the three types of wholesome conduct?"
He replied, "It takes the ten paths of wholesome action as its basis.
He asked again:
"What is the foundation of the ten paths of wholesome action?
He replied, "It is taking the restraint of the six sense faculties as its foundation."
He asked again:
"What is the foundation for gathering the six sense faculties? He replied:
"Right mindfulness is the foundation.
He asked again:
"What is the foundation of right mindfulness?"
He replied, "Right contemplation is the foundation.
He asked again:
“What is the basis of right contemplation? He replied,
“Its basis is firm mindfulness and non-forgetfulness.”
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī, how many minds does a bodhisattva possess that are able to encompass the cause and able to encompass the fruit?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra! Bodhisattvas possess four minds that can encompass the cause and can encompass the fruit."

What are the four? First, the mind of initial resolve; second, the mind that practices the path; third, the mind of non-retrogression; and fourth, the mind of the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood.
The initial resolve serves as the causal condition for the mind that practices the path;
the mind that practices the path serves as the causal condition for the mind of non-retrogression;
and the mind of non-retrogression serves as the causal condition for the mind of the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood.

"Furthermore, O Devaputra, you should know this: the initial aspiration is like sowing seeds in a field; the mind practicing the path is like the growth of those seeds; the mind of non-retrogression is like the first formation of flowers and fruit; and the mind of the stage of succession is like the utility of those flowers and fruits."

Furthermore, the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment is like a carpenter gathering materials; the mind practicing the path is like using an adze to shape the wood; the mind of non-retrogression is like securely installing the materials; and the mind of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood is like the completion of the carriage for transport.

Furthermore, the mind that first resolves for enlightenment is like the newly risen moon; the mind that practices the path is like the moon on the fifth day; the mind of non-retrogression is like the moon on the tenth day; the mind of being in the final birth before Buddhahood is like the moon on the fourteenth day; and the wisdom of a Tathāgata is like the moon on the fifteenth day.

Furthermore, the initial aspiration for enlightenment can transcend the stage of the śrāvaka; the mind that practices the path can transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddha; the mind of non-retrogression can transcend the stage of indetermination; and the mind of the "one-life-to-birth" stage dwells securely in the stage of certainty.

Furthermore, the mind that first resolves upon enlightenment is like studying the first chapter; the mind that practices the path is like studying the second chapter; the mind of non-retrogression is like being able to apply the chapters in practice; and the mind of the stage of "one-life-to-buddhahood" is like attaining mastery of the profound sutras.

Furthermore, the initial resolve arises from causes; the mind that practices the path arises from wisdom; the non-retrogressive mind arises from abandonment; and the mind of the stage of succession arises from the fruit.

Furthermore, there is the causal power of the initial resolve, the mental power of practicing the path, the power of severing [defilements] through the non-retrogressive mind, and the resultant power of the mind of the stage of being one-for-all-births (ekajātipratibaddha).

Furthermore, the initial aspiration is like a sick person seeking medicine; the mind practicing the path is like discerning the medicine; the mind of non-retrogression is like the sick person taking the medicine; and the mind of the stage of being next in succession is like the sick person recovering from the illness.

Furthermore, the mind first resolved upon awakening is born into the family of the Dharma Kings; the mind practicing the path studies the Dharma of the Dharma Kings; the non-retrogressive mind is able to fully master the study of the Dharma of the Dharma Kings;
and the mind of the stage of succession (the penultimate birth) studies the Dharma of the Dharma Kings and attains mastery.
At that time, within the great assembly, there was a devaputra named King of Steadfast Radiance, who was non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Devaputra Samādhiprabhāsamati addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What is the concise path of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
By means of this concise path, one swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra!
There are two concise paths for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by means of these concise paths, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these two? First is skillful means (upāya), and second is wisdom (prajñā).
Gathering wholesome dharmas is called skillful means; analyzing and dispersing all dharmas is called wisdom.
Furthermore, skillful means is called following the conduct of sentient beings, while wisdom is called not turning back from the characteristics of all phenomena;
skillful means is called responding to the minds of sentient beings, while wisdom is called not depending on any phenomena;
skillful means is called the harmonious integration of all phenomena, while wisdom is called the relinquishing of all phenomena.
Skillful means is called the arising of causes and conditions; wisdom is called the cessation of causes and conditions.
Skillful means is called knowing the distinctions among all phenomena; wisdom is called the non-differentiation of the nature of phenomena.
Skillful means is called adorning the Buddha-fields; wisdom is called adorning the Buddha-fields without making any distinctions.
Skillful means refers to knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings; wisdom refers to not apprehending sentient beings.
Skillful means refers to being able to reach the site of enlightenment; wisdom refers to being able to attain all Buddha-dharmas.
“Son of Heaven, you should know that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess two paths; by means of these two paths, they swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these two? First is the path of assistance, and second is the path of abandonment.
The path of assistance consists of the five pāramitās; the path of abandonment is the prajñāpāramitā.
“Furthermore, there are two paths. What are the two?
First is the path with fetters; second is the path without fetters.”
The path with attachment consists of the five *pāramitās*, while the path without attachment is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, there are two paths:
first, the limited path; second, the limitless path.
The path with measure involves grasping at signs and conceptual differentiation; the immeasurable path does not involve grasping at signs or conceptual differentiation.
"Furthermore, there are two paths:
first, the path of wisdom; second, the path of abandonment."
"The path of wisdom extends from the first stage to the seventh stage; the path of abandonment extends from the eighth stage to the tenth stage.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Anuvicāraśūravikrama who asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, "What is the meaning of 'bodhisattva'?"
"What is meant by the wisdom of a bodhisattva? Mañjuśrī replied, "Noble son!..."
"Meaning" (artha) is called useless; "knowledge" (jñāna) is called useful.
What is meant by "meaning is called useless"?
Meaning is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); as an unconditioned dharma, it is neither useful nor non-useful toward other dharmas.

Furthermore, "meaning" (artha) is neither the characteristic of defilement nor the characteristic of detachment; this meaning is neither functional nor non-functional with respect to phenomena (dharma).
Moreover, meaning neither increases nor decreases; it is neither functional nor non-functional with respect to phenomena.
"Son of Heaven, what is meant by wisdom?
Wisdom is the path of forbearance; it is that which the mind employs, not something useless.
Therefore, wisdom is called useful, not useless."
The merit of wisdom lies in its power to sever [delusion]; therefore, wisdom is called functional and not non-functional.

Wisdom is defined as the skillful knowledge of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and what is possible and what is impossible; therefore, wisdom is called functional and not non-functional.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra, Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of knowledge.

What are these ten? First is the knowledge of causes; second is the knowledge of results; third is the knowledge of meaning; fourth is the knowledge of skillful means; fifth is the knowledge of wisdom; sixth is the knowledge of gathering [disciples]; seventh is the knowledge of the perfections (pāramitās); eighth is the knowledge of great compassion; ninth is the knowledge of maturing sentient beings; and tenth is the knowledge of non-attachment to all phenomena."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
All bodhisattvas have ten types of emergence. What are these ten?
First is the arousal of the body, because he wishes to cause the bodily karma of sentient beings to be pure;
second is the arousal of speech, because he wishes to cause the verbal karma of sentient beings to be pure;
third is the arousal of the mind, because he wishes to cause the mental karma of sentient beings to be pure.
Fourth is internal manifestation, because of non-attachment to all internal things;
fifth is external manifestation, because of the desire to cause sentient beings to abide in right practice;
sixth is the manifestation of wisdom, because of being fully endowed with the Buddha-wisdom.
Seventh is the arousal of loving-kindness, because of recollecting all adornments of merit;
eighth is the arousal for the maturation of sentient beings, because of guarding the medicine of wisdom;
ninth is the arousal of conditioned knowledge, because of being fully endowed with the accumulation of concentration.
Tenth is the arousal of unconditioned wisdom, because the mind does not cling to the triple world.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven,
all bodhisattvas have ten practices.

What are the ten? First, the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*); second, the practice of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); third, the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, the practice of skillful means (*upāya*); fifth, the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); sixth, the practice of seeking the dharmas that assist wisdom; seventh, the practice of seeking the dharmas of knowledge (*jñāna*); eighth, the practice of mental purity; ninth, the practice of contemplating the truths (*satya*); and tenth, the practice of non-attachment to all that is beloved.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
Bodhisattvas also have ten further contemplations on exhaustion. What are these ten?

First, contemplation on the exhaustion of phenomena; second, contemplation on the exhaustion of sensation; third, contemplation on the exhaustion of dharmas; fourth, contemplation on the exhaustion of afflictions; fifth, contemplation on the exhaustion of views; sixth, contemplation on the exhaustion of the heterodox; seventh, contemplation on the exhaustion of craving; eighth, contemplation on the exhaustion of non-attachment; ninth, contemplation on the exhaustion of fetters and latent tendencies; tenth, contemplation on the exhaustion of attachment to the practices of the site of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
Bodhisattvas have ten further methods of cultivation. What are these ten?
First, it remedies the mind of stinginess and greed by raining down the rain of giving;
second, it remedies the mind of broken precepts through the purity of the three dharmas;
third, it remedies the mind of anger by practicing loving-kindness and patience.
Fourth, it remedies the mind of indolence, because one seeks the Buddha-dharma without weariness;
fifth, it remedies the mind of unwholesome vitarka and vicāra, because one attains mastery over dhyāna, samādhi, and liberation;
sixth, it remedies the mind of ignorance, because it gives rise to the dharmas that assist the definitive Prajñāpāramitā.
Seventh, it is to subdue the mind of various afflictions by generating the factors that assist the path;
eighth, it is to subdue the mind of inverted paths by cultivating the factors that assist the Four Noble Truths;
ninth, it is to subdue the mind so that one acts with mastery regarding both the timely and the untimely.
Tenth is the contemplation that treats [the self] as a disease,
because there is no self-nature in phenomena. Furthermore, O Devaputra,
bodhisattvas have another ten stages of goodness.
What are the ten? First is excellence of body, because of being free from the three evils of the body;
second is excellence of speech, because of being free from the four evils of speech.
Third is excellence of mind, because it is free from the three evils of the mind;
fourth is internal excellence, because one does not cling to the view of a self;
fifth is external excellence, because one does not cling to any phenomena.
Sixth is the goodness of non-attachment to the factors that assist wisdom, because one does not crave the dharmas that aid the path;
seventh is the goodness of not exalting oneself, because one contemplates the nature of the noble path;
eighth is the goodness of eliminating [clinging to] the body, because one cultivates and accumulates the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Ninth is the goodness of being free from inversion, because it does not deceive any sentient beings;
tenth is the goodness of not begrudging one's body or life, because one transforms sentient beings through great compassion.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
Those bodhisattvas who value practicing in accordance with the Dharma are able to attain Bodhi; it is not those who do not value practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
To practice in accordance with the Dharma means to act according to what has been taught."
"One who does not practice in accordance with the Dharma possesses only words, yet cannot act as they have spoken.
Furthermore, O Devaputra, there are two further ways in which Bodhisattvas practice in accordance with the Dharma."
What are these two? First, the practice of the path; second, the practice of abandonment.
Furthermore, there are two types of practitioners who follow the Dharma.
What are these two? First, personally practicing what is wholesome; second, teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two ways of practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
What are these two? First, the practice of wisdom; second, the non-practice of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two types of followers of the Dharma.
What are these two? First, skillfully discerning the various stages; second, not discerning between stage and non-stage.
Furthermore, there are two types of practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What are these two?
First, knowing the faults of the various stages while being able to advance further;
second, skillfully knowing how to achieve full perfection as one proceeds from one stage to the next.
Furthermore, there are two types of those who practice in accordance with the Dharma. What are the two?
First, those who skillfully know the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; [the second is those who skillfully know the path of the bodhisattvas].
"Second, they skillfully know the Buddha-way and practice the conduct of non-retrogression.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You have been able to explain the path of fundamental karma for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is exactly as you have said.
When this Dharma was spoken, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, and all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and received it with faith.
The Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra (The Sūtra on the Inquiry of Mañjuśrī Concerning Bodhi)
